title: Cost of Goods Sold, Gross Profit and Special Items
summary: The four-step calculation of cost of goods sold and gross profit, two worked examples and how to treat carriage, wages, returns and discounts.

p: Cost of goods sold = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses − closing stock. Net purchases = purchases − returns outwards + carriage inwards.

Step 1: net purchases. Step 2: cost of goods available = opening stock + net purchases + direct expenses. Step 3: cost of goods sold = cost of goods available − closing stock. Step 4: gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold, where net sales = sales − returns inwards.
Opening stock ₦30,000; purchases ₦150,000; returns outwards ₦5,000; carriage inwards ₦8,000; closing stock ₦40,000; sales ₦250,000; returns inwards ₦10,000.

sections.h: Example 2: Taiwo Enterprises, year ended 31 December 2024
p: Balances: opening stock 25,000; purchases 180,000; sales 320,000; returns inwards 12,000; returns outwards 8,000; carriage inwards 6,500; carriage outwards 4,200; factory wages 35,000; office wages 28,000; import duty 9,500; closing stock 38,000.

sections.h: What was left out, and why
p: Carriage outwards ₦4,200 is a selling expense, so it goes to the profit and loss account. Office wages ₦28,000 are an administrative expense, so they go to the profit and loss account. Factory wages ₦35,000 are a direct expense, so they go in the trading account. Import duty ₦9,500 is part of the cost of the goods, so it goes in the trading account.

Carriage inwards (on purchases): the cost of bringing goods in; it is part of the cost of goods and goes in the trading account. Carriage outwards (on sales): the cost of delivering goods to customers; it is a selling expense and goes in the profit and loss account.
Wages: factory wages are direct labour and go in the trading account; office wages are administrative and go in the profit and loss account.
Returns: returns inwards are deducted from sales; returns outwards are deducted from purchases.

Trade discount: a reduction in the list price, already deducted before recording, so it is not recorded in the books. Cash discount: given for early payment and recorded in the books; it goes to the profit and loss account, not the trading account.
Drawings in goods: when the owner takes goods for personal use, purchases are reduced (Dr Drawings, Cr Purchases) before the trading account is prepared.

title: The Profit and Loss Account: Meaning, Format and Items
summary: What the profit and loss account is, gross profit compared with net profit, its purposes, format and how expenses are classified.

p: The profit and loss account is an account prepared to find the net profit or net loss of a business by comparing all income with all expenses. It is the second part of the final accounts, after the trading account. The link is: trading account → gross profit → profit and loss account → net profit.
Net profit is what remains after deducting all expenses from total income. Net loss arises when expenses are more than income.

Gross profit comes from trading only (sales less cost of goods sold) and is shown in the trading account. Net profit is the overall profit after ALL expenses: gross profit + other income − all expenses. It is shown in the profit and loss account.

1. To find the net profit or loss. 2. To show how the gross profit was used and what the other income and expenses were. 3. To provide a basis for tax. 4. To judge performance and control of expenses by comparing periods. 5. To help decisions on expansion, costs, pricing and investment. 6. To inform owners, lenders and management.
Study the table. If total expenses exceed total income, the result is a net loss.

head: Profit and loss account for the year ended ...
rows: Add: other income (commission received, discount received, rent received, interest received, profit on sale of an asset)
Less: expenses (salaries, rent, rates, insurance, electricity, telephone, stationery, bad debts, discount allowed, depreciation, carriage outwards, interest paid, advertising)

p: Debit side (expenses). Administrative expenses: office salaries, rent, rates, insurance, stationery, telephone, postage, printing, legal fees, audit fees, general expenses. Selling and distribution expenses: advertising, sales commission, carriage outwards, delivery expenses, packaging, marketing, sales promotion. Financial expenses: interest paid, bank charges, loan and overdraft interest. Other expenses: bad debts, discount allowed, depreciation, loss on sale of an asset, donations, fines.

Credit side (income). Gross profit, then other income: commission received, discount received, rent received, interest received, dividend received, profit on sale of an asset, bad debts recovered. Net profit is the balancing figure and is transferred to the capital account.
By nature: direct expenses (factory wages, import duty, carriage inwards) go in the trading account. Indirect expenses (office salaries, rent, electricity) go in the profit and loss account.
By function: administrative, selling, distribution and financial expenses.
By behaviour: fixed expenses do not change with sales (rent, salaries, insurance). Variable expenses change with sales (sales commission, carriage outwards).

Discount allowed is given to customers, reduces income and is debited. Discount received comes from suppliers, increases income and is credited. Carriage inwards is in the trading account. Carriage outwards is in the profit and loss account.

sections.h: Transfer of the net profit to capital
p: Net profit belongs to the owner, so it increases capital. Journal: Dr Profit and loss account ₦56,000; Cr Capital account ₦56,000. In the capital account, drawings are deducted. Capital account: opening balance ₦275,000, add net profit ₦56,000, less drawings ₦25,000, closing capital ₦306,000.

A net loss does the opposite: Dr Capital, Cr Profit and loss account. For example, with capital of ₦150,000, a net loss of ₦20,000 and drawings of ₦25,000, the closing capital is 150,000 − 20,000 − 25,000 = ₦105,000.

The balance sheet check: assets are buildings 120,000, motor vehicles 60,000, furniture 40,000, closing stock 42,000, debtors 55,000, bank 28,000 and cash 3,000, which total ₦348,000. Capital ₦306,000 plus creditors ₦42,000 also equals ₦348,000. The balance sheet balances.

The trial balance feeds the trading account, which gives the gross profit; this goes to the profit and loss account, which gives the net profit; this goes to the capital account; and the closing capital goes to the balance sheet.

title: Adjustments: Closing Stock, Prepayments and Accruals
summary: Why adjustments are made, how closing stock, prepaid expenses and accrued expenses are treated, and a formula for the expense of the year.

p: Adjustments are changes made at the end of the period so that the profit is accurate and the financial position is true. They apply the accrual concept: income and expenses are recorded in the period to which they belong, not when cash is paid or received. Common adjustments are closing stock, prepayments, accruals, depreciation, provision for bad debts, bad debts written off, accrued interest and goods taken for own use.

Closing stock is the value of the goods not sold at the end of the period. It is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV). Cost is the purchase price plus costs of bringing the stock to its present state. NRV is the selling price less the costs of making the sale. Example: stock cost ₦50,000, NRV ₦45,000: value at ₦45,000. Stock cost ₦50,000, NRV ₦60,000: value at ₦50,000.

If the closing stock is already in the trial balance, it is shown only in the balance sheet as an asset. If the closing stock is given as an adjustment (not in the trial balance), it appears in TWO places: in the trading account (deducted from the cost of goods) and in the balance sheet (current assets).
Journal: Dr Stock account ₦40,000, Cr Trading account ₦40,000 (being closing stock recorded).

A prepaid expense has been paid in the current period for a benefit in a future period. Examples: rent paid for next year, an insurance premium for the next period, subscriptions and rates paid in advance. Treatment: deduct the prepayment from the amount paid to find the expense, and show the prepayment as a current asset.
Example: rent paid ₦120,000, of which ₦20,000 is for next year. Profit and loss account: rent ₦100,000. Balance sheet: prepaid rent ₦20,000 (current asset).

Detailed example: insurance of ₦36,000 was paid on 1 April 2024 for one year; the year ends on 31 December. The monthly premium is 36,000 ÷ 12 = ₦3,000. The 2024 expense is 9 months = ₦27,000. The prepayment for 2025 is 3 months = ₦9,000. Journal: Dr Profit and loss ₦27,000; Dr Prepaid insurance ₦9,000; Cr Insurance ₦36,000.

An accrued expense has been incurred in the period but not yet paid. Examples: salaries earned but unpaid, rent due but unpaid, electricity used but not billed, interest owing. Treatment: add the outstanding amount to the amount paid to find the expense, and show it as a current liability.
Example: salaries paid ₦480,000, outstanding ₦40,000. Profit and loss account: salaries ₦520,000. Balance sheet: outstanding salaries ₦40,000 (current liability).

Detailed example: rent is ₦10,000 a month and was paid up to November; December is unpaid. Paid 11 months: ₦110,000; outstanding ₦10,000; expense ₦120,000. Journal: Dr Profit and loss ₦120,000; Cr Bank ₦110,000; Cr Outstanding rent ₦10,000.
The general rule is: expense for the year = cash paid in the year + opening prepayment − closing prepayment − opening accrual + closing accrual.

Example: rent paid during the year ₦144,000; rent prepaid at the start of the year ₦12,000 (it was paid last year but belongs to this year); rent outstanding at the end ₦15,000; no prepayment at the end. Expense = 144,000 + 12,000 + 15,000 = ₦171,000. The profit and loss account is charged ₦171,000; the balance sheet shows outstanding rent of ₦15,000 as a liability.

title: Adjustments: Depreciation, Provision for Bad Debts and Bad Debts
summary: Why and how assets are depreciated (straight-line and reducing balance), the provision for depreciation, provisions for doubtful debts (new, increased and decreased), and bad debts written off or recovered.

p: Depreciation is the systematic spreading of the cost of a fixed asset over its useful life. We provide for it because assets lose value over time, to match the cost with the income they help to earn, to show the true value of assets, and to follow the accrual and prudence concepts.
Causes: wear and tear, obsolescence (becoming out of date), the passage of time and depletion (for natural resources like a mine).

Straight-line method: the same amount every year. Annual depreciation = (cost − scrap value) ÷ useful life, or cost × rate. Example: cost ₦100,000, scrap value ₦10,000, life 10 years. Depreciation = (100,000 − 10,000) ÷ 10 = ₦9,000 a year.

Reducing balance method: a fixed percentage of the book value (cost less depreciation so far). It gives more depreciation in the early years. Example: cost ₦100,000, rate 20%. Year 1: 20% of 100,000 = ₦20,000. Year 2: 20% of 80,000 = ₦16,000. Year 3: 20% of 64,000 = ₦12,800.

Method A: reduce the asset directly. Method B (better): keep the asset at cost and build up a provision for depreciation account, so that the balance sheet shows cost, total depreciation to date and net book value. Example: machinery at cost ₦100,000; less provision for depreciation ₦20,000; net book value ₦80,000.

Journal each year: Dr Depreciation account (expense) ₦20,000; Cr Provision for depreciation ₦20,000. The depreciation account is then transferred to the profit and loss account. In Year 2 the provision account carries ₦20,000 from Year 1 plus ₦20,000 for the year, giving ₦40,000.

A provision is an amount set aside out of profit for debts that may not be paid. It follows the prudence concept. A specific provision is for named debtors likely to default. A general provision is a percentage of all debtors, based on experience.
New provision: debtors ₦100,000, provision 5% = ₦5,000. Profit and loss account: provision ₦5,000. Balance sheet: debtors ₦100,000 less provision ₦5,000 = net debtors ₦95,000.
Increase: old provision ₦5,000; debtors ₦120,000; new provision at 5% = ₦6,000. Only the increase of ₦1,000 is charged to the profit and loss account (Dr Profit and loss, Cr Provision).
Decrease: old provision ₦5,000; debtors ₦80,000; new provision at 5% = ₦4,000. The decrease of ₦1,000 is added to profit (Dr Provision, Cr Profit and loss).

A bad debt is a debt that is definitely lost and must be written off. A provision is an estimate of a loss that may happen. To write off a bad debt: Dr Bad debts, Cr the debtor. It is an expense in the profit and loss account, and debtors are reduced in the balance sheet.
If a debt written off is later recovered: Dr Bank, Cr Bad debts recovered (income).

sections.h: Bad debts and the provision together
p: Example: debtors ₦150,000; bad debts to write off ₦10,000; provision of 5% of the remaining debtors; old provision ₦6,000. Step 1: debtors after write-off 150,000 − 10,000 = ₦140,000. Step 2: new provision 5% × 140,000 = ₦7,000. Step 3: increase = 7,000 − 6,000 = ₦1,000. Profit and loss: bad debts ₦10,000 and increase in provision ₦1,000. Balance sheet: debtors ₦140,000 less provision ₦7,000 = ₦133,000.

Items: rent ₦36,000 with ₦6,000 prepaid; insurance ₦18,000 with ₦3,000 outstanding; salaries ₦72,000 with ₦8,000 outstanding; motor vehicles at cost ₦120,000, provision for depreciation ₦30,000, depreciation 20% on cost; debtors ₦80,000 with ₦5,000 to be written off; old provision ₦4,000, new provision 5% of debtors.

title: A Comprehensive Example with Adjustments
summary: Preparing the trading account, the profit and loss account and the balance sheet extract for Amina Enterprises using six adjustments.

p: Amina Enterprises trial balance at 31 December 2024. Debit: drawings 30,000; premises 150,000; motor vehicles 80,000; furniture 50,000; stock (1 January) 40,000; purchases 220,000; debtors 60,000; bank 25,000; salaries 60,000; rent 24,000; insurance 12,000. Credit: sales 400,000; creditors 45,000; provision for bad debts 3,000; provision for depreciation, motor vehicles 20,000; provision for depreciation, furniture 10,000; capital.

Adjustments: (1) closing stock ₦48,000; (2) rent prepaid ₦4,000; (3) salaries outstanding ₦5,000; (4) depreciate motor vehicles 20%; (5) depreciate furniture 10%; (6) keep the provision for bad debts at 5% of debtors.

Rent: paid 24,000 less prepaid 4,000 = ₦20,000. Salaries: paid 60,000 plus outstanding 5,000 = ₦65,000. Depreciation of motor vehicles: 20% × cost ₦80,000 = ₦16,000; total provision 20,000 + 16,000 = ₦36,000; net book value ₦44,000. Depreciation of furniture: 10% × ₦50,000 = ₦5,000; total provision 10,000 + 5,000 = ₦15,000; net book value ₦35,000. Provision for bad debts: 5% × 60,000 = ₦3,000, the same as the old provision, so there is no charge.
